content: Historically, children and adolescents with intellectual disabilities were not expected to learn to read and were excluded from reading instruction. However, societal expectations have shifted over the past few decades, and it is now recognized that these individuals should be provided with literacy instruction and can benefit from it. This change has led to an increase in research focused on identifying effective interventions to improve beginning reading skills in this population. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions designed to teach beginning reading skills to children and adolescents with intellectual disabilities. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple electronic databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, up to October 2019. They also reviewed reference lists, contacted study authors, and used Google Scholar to identify additional studies. The review included randomized controlled trials (including quasi-randomized trials) that involved children and adolescents aged 4 to 21 years with intellectual disabilities, defined as having an intelligence quotient (IQ) two standard deviations or more below the population mean. The trials compared beginning reading interventions to control conditions, such as no treatment, wait-list controls, usual treatment, attention controls, or alternative non-reading instruction. Two independent reviewers screened the studies for inclusion, extracted data using a standardized form, and assessed the risk of bias and quality of evidence using the GRADE approach. When data were missing, the reviewers contacted study authors for additional information. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted to combine effect sizes for primary and secondary outcomes, with results presented as standardized mean differences (SMD) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). The review identified seven studies involving 352 children and adolescents with intellectual disabilities that met the inclusion criteria. All interventions were delivered in school settings. Four studies were conducted in the United States, one in Canada, and two in the United Kingdom. Three studies were funded by the US Department of Education, one by Canadian research organizations, and three did not report funding sources. Some concerns about bias were noted, particularly due to challenges in blinding participants, personnel, and outcome assessors. The meta-analyses revealed small-to-moderate effects of beginning reading interventions on several outcomes. For the primary outcomes, moderate effect sizes were observed for phonologic awareness (SMD 0.55, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.86; 4 studies, 178 participants; moderate-quality evidence), word reading (SMD 0.54, 95% CI 0.05 to 1.03; 5 studies, 220 participants; moderate-quality evidence), and decoding (SMD 0.40, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.67; 5 studies, 230 participants; low-quality evidence). No adverse events were reported in any of the studies. For the secondary outcomes, a moderate effect size was found for oral reading fluency (SMD 0.65, 95% CI –0.12 to 1.42; 2 studies, 84 participants; low-quality evidence) and language skills (SMD 0.28, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.54; 3 studies, 222 participants; moderate-quality evidence). The authors concluded that beginning reading interventions incorporating phonologic awareness, letter-sound instruction, and decoding are associated with small-to-moderate improvements in phonologic awareness, word reading, decoding, oral reading fluency, and language skills in children and adolescents with intellectual disabilities. These findings are consistent with prior research on reading interventions for individuals without intellectual disabilities.
